original_value: AbstractContemporary developments, such as digital Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and wearable devices estimating sleep, could support the implementation of CBT for insomnia at a large scale. We assessed what characterizes those users who connected a wearable device to the program to estimate sleep diary variables, and whether connecting a wearable device affected insomnia symptom improvement, related well-being, and program interaction. In total, 3551 users (63% female, mean age 44.50 ± 14.78 years) of a dCBT program who completed a post-therapy survey, including 378 users (10.6%) who used a device, were selected. Within-subject, pre-therapy to post-therapy, the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI, 7 Items) was used to assess insomnia. Two-item measures (depression, anxiety) and single item measures (perceived stress, life satisfaction, work productivity) of well-being were analyzed, in addition to program interaction. For all participants, insomnia symptoms significantly improved following dCBT (t(3504) = 83.33, p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 1.45), as did depression and anxiety symptoms, perceived stress, life satisfaction and work productivity. Those who did not connect a device reported better sleep and less affected work productivity (all p < .001) than those who did connect a device at baseline and post-treatment; nevertheless treatment effects were largely similar for the two groups. Those who connected a device interacted more with additional program components. In conclusion, improvements in insomnia after completing dCBT are similar in persons choosing to wear a wearable device to estimate sleep and persons completing a subjective sleep diary. Potentially, use of wearable devices can facilitate treatment for those who struggle to complete daily diaries.

result.paraphrase: Abstract developments such as digital Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and wearable devices that estimate sleep may help scale CBT for insomnia. We examined which users connected a wearable device to the program to estimate sleep diary variables, and whether device use influenced improvement in insomnia symptoms, related well-being, and program engagement. Overall, 3551 users of a dCBT program who completed a post-therapy survey were included; 378 of them (10.6%) used a device. The sample had 63% female users, with a mean age of 44.50 ± 14.78 years. Insomnia was assessed with the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI, 7 items) using pre-therapy and post-therapy within-subject comparisons. In addition to program interaction, well-being was evaluated with two-item measures of depression and anxiety and single-item measures of perceived stress, life satisfaction, and work productivity. Across all participants, insomnia symptoms improved significantly after dCBT (t(3504) = 83.33, p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 1.45), along with depression, anxiety, perceived stress, life satisfaction, and work productivity. Participants who did not connect a device reported better sleep and less impaired work productivity at both baseline and post-treatment than those who did connect a device (all p < .001); however, treatment effects were largely comparable between the two groups. Device users interacted more with additional program components. In summary, insomnia improvements after completing dCBT were similar for people who chose to wear a device to estimate sleep and those who completed a subjective sleep diary. Wearable devices may therefore help support treatment for people who have difficulty completing daily diaries.
